paragraphs.text: A written account of the history of the time of distress that occurred in Edessa, Amida, and all Mesopotamia.

I received the letters of your God-loving Reverence, O most excellent of men, Sergius, priest and abbot, in which you instructed me to write for you, as a memorial, when the locusts came, when the sun grew dark, and when the earthquake, famine, pestilence, and war between the Romans and Persians occurred. Along with these things, however, your letters also contained lavish praises of me. These put me in great conflict with myself, since not one of them is actually borne out by my conduct. I, however, wished to write about your qualities, but the eye of my mind was unable to contemplate and see as it truly is the wonderful robe that your diligent will has woven for you and clothed you in. For you have clearly shown that you burn with love, which fulfills the law. For you have cared not only for the brothers who are under your authority at present, but also for all lovers of learning who will enter your blessed monastery. In your zeal, you wish to leave written records of the chastisements that have occurred at various times because of our sins, so that, when they read and see what happened to us, they may guard against our sins and escape our punishments. I never cease or grow weary of marveling at the fullness of your love, which overflows toward everyone. Yet I cannot describe it as it truly is, since I have not come close to practicing it. Nor do I know how to recount it on the basis of the conversation you once had with me.

Like Jonathan, that faithful friend, you bound yourself to me in love. Yet the attachment of Jonathan’s soul to David’s soul was not as great as this, when he saw that the mighty warrior had been killed by David’s hands and the army had been delivered, because he loved him for his good deeds. You, however, though you saw nothing good in me, loved me more than yourself. Even Jonathan’s rescue of David from death at Saul’s hands is not as worthy of wonder as this deed of yours, since he was only repaying something he owed him. For David had first rescued him from death and granted life to him and his father’s entire household, so that they would not die at the hands of the Philistine. Although I have done nothing like this for you, you are constantly pleading with God on my behalf, that I may be rescued from Satan and that he may not kill me through sins. Rather, it is fitting to say this: you have loved me as David loved Saul [?]. You are so intoxicated by the abundance of your love that, in the fervor of your love, you do not even recognize my limitations, but think things of me that are beyond me. For in the past you supplied what I lacked through the instruction in your letters, and you cared for me like parents, who, although they have received no benefit from their children, attend to everything their children need. Now, however, in your wisdom you have humbled yourself and asked me to write for you things that are beyond my ability, so that through this very act you may become still greater: although you know these things better than I do, you wish to learn them from me. Nor do I begrudge you this or draw back from what you have commanded.

But know that I too, when I saw these signs taking place and the chastisements coming after them, I thought they deserved to be written down and preserved in memory, and not left to be forgotten. But when I considered the weakness of my understanding and my own lack of learning, I held back from this. Now that you have instructed me to undertake this very task, I am as afraid as someone who does not know how to swim well and is ordered to descend into deep water. But because I trust in your uplifting prayers, which you continually send to God on my behalf, I believe that I will be lifted out of the sea into which you have thrown me, kept safe from drowning. I swim in its shallows as best I can, because its depth cannot be fathomed. For who is capable of recounting properly the things God does in his wisdom to put an end to sins and to discipline wrongdoing? For the precise workings of God's providence are hidden even from the angels. You can learn this from the parable of the weeds in the Gospel. For when the servants said to the master of the house, “Do you want us to go and gather them up?” he, who knew things as they really were, said to them, “No, because while you are gathering the weeds, you might uproot the wheat along with them.” But this much we can say according to our knowledge: because of our many sins, our punishments have come repeatedly. And if God's protection were not holding the world together to keep it from falling apart, the lives of all human beings would already have come to an end. For in what times have afflictions like these occurred in such rapid succession, except in these times in which we now live? And because their cause has not ceased, they too have not yet ceased. Besides what we have seen with our own eyes, heard with our own ears, and are experiencing, reports from far and near have also terrified us: disasters that occurred in one place after another, terrible earthquakes, the destruction of cities, famines and plagues, wars and disturbances, the capture and exile of the inhabitants of whole regions, and the demolition and burning of churches. Astonished yourself at how many these were, you wrote asking me to record them in words of sorrow and lamentation that would astonish readers and listeners. I know that you said this out of your zeal for what is good, so that those who hear these things might also feel remorse and turn to repentance.

But know that writing in a moving way is one thing, and writing truthfully is another. For anyone who possesses natural eloquence can, if he wishes, write sorrowful and moving accounts. But I am unskilled in speech, and in this book I record only those things that everyone in our region attests are true. It is up to those who read or hear them to examine them and, if they wish, turn to repentance. But perhaps someone will say, “What benefit do these things offer their readers if words of admonition are not mixed into them?” For my part, since I am unable to do this, I say that these punishments that have come upon us are sufficient to set us and those who come after us on the right path, and also, through remembering and reading about them, to teach us that they were sent upon us because of our sins. If they did not teach us this, they would indeed be of no benefit to us. But that cannot be said. For all the believers under heaven testify that afflictions serve to instruct us and that they are sent upon us because of our sins. They agree with the words of the blessed Paul, who said, “When we are judged by our Lord, we are being disciplined so that we may not be condemned with the world.” For all the discipline that people receive in this world is intended to restrain them from their sins and make the judgment of the world to come easier for them. And those who are disciplined because of wrongdoers, although they themselves have not sinned, receive a double reward. But the mercy that is always shown even to those who are unworthy comes from God's kindness, grace, and patience, for he wishes this world to endure until the time determined in his unfailing knowledge. And that these things are so— this is evident from the proofs in the Holy Scriptures and from the events that happened among us, which we have undertaken to record.

For the hardships of famine, and also of pestilence during the time of the locusts, pressed upon us until we were close to slipping into destruction. But God had mercy on us, although we were unworthy, and gave us a little respite from the afflictions that had come upon us in succession. This, as I said, was because of his grace. After we had recovered our breath, however, he changed the scourges with which he afflicted us and struck us through the Assyrian, who is called the rod of wrath. Yet when I say that God struck us through the Persians, I am not denying their free will, nor am I laying upon God the blame for their insolence. Rather, because I consider that he did not exact retribution from them on account of our sins, I have stated that he struck us through them. For the intention of that wicked people is shown especially clearly in their failure to show mercy to those who were handed over to them. For they habitually displayed their own will and rejoiced in people's misfortune. The prophet also reproaches them for this very thing when, prophesying about the destruction of Babylon, he speaks as though from the mouth of the Lord: “I was angry with my people, who defiled my inheritance, and I handed them over to you, but you showed them no mercy.” So they also harmed us in this way, acting of their own will and without mercy, as is their custom. For although the rod of their blows did not reach our own bodies, and they were unable to gain control of our city— since the promise Christ made to the believing King Abgar could not be annulled, when he said, “Your city shall be blessed, and no enemy shall ever rule over it”—nevertheless, through the believers who were plundered, taken captive, killed, and laid waste in the other cities that were conquered, and who became like mud in the streets, all those who had learned to suffer with those who suffer tasted [?] suffering in no small measure. Others, who were far removed from such sympathy, were tormented by fear for their own lives because of their lack of faith, supposing that the enemy would gain control of Edessa as he had of the other cities. These are the things about which we are going to write to you.

But since, according to the words of wise Solomon, “War is brought about by provocation,” and you wish to learn precisely this— what causes provoked it—I wish to explain briefly to you where the causes arose, even if it seems that I am speaking about matters whose time has passed. Then, a little later, I will also explain to you when the war gained strength from those causes. For although this war was stirred up against us because of our sins, it took its occasion from outward events. These are the things I want to relate to you, so that you may have a clear understanding of this matter, and not be drawn in with foolish people to blame the ruler, the faithful emperor Anastasius. For he was not the originator of the war. Rather, it had been brewing for a long time, as you can understand from what I am writing to you.

The Romans built the city of Nisibis in the year 609, and it remained under their rule for sixty-five years. After the death of Julian in Persia, which occurred in the year 674, Jovian, who succeeded him as emperor of the Romans, valued peace above everything else. For this reason, he allowed the Persians to rule Nisibis for a period of one hundred and twenty years, after which they were to return it to its owners. These years came to an end in the time of Zeno, emperor of the Romans. The Persians were unwilling to return the city, and this matter stirred up a dispute.

There was also a treaty between the Romans and the Persians that, if they needed one another whenever they were at war with any nation, they would help one another, by providing three hundred fighting men with their weapons and horses, or three hundred staters in place of each man. This was to be according to the wishes of the side in need. Now the Romans, with the help of God, the Lord of all, had no need of help from the Persians. For faithful emperors had occupied the throne from that time until now, and their rule was strengthened by help from heaven. The Persian kings, however, used to send envoys and receive gold because of their need. They did not receive it as tribute, as many people supposed.

For in our own days, Peroz, king of the Persians, received gold from the Romans many times because of his wars with the Chionites, who are the Huns. He did not do so by demanding tribute, but by insisting to them that he was fighting his battles on their behalf, “so that,” he said, “they will not cross into your country.” His claim was made credible by the slaughter and captivity that the Huns had inflicted in Roman territory, in the year 707, in the days of the emperors Honorius and Arcadius, the sons of Theodosius the Great. All Syria had been delivered into their hands through the treachery of Rufinus the prefect and the negligence of Addaeus the general.

With the help of the gold he had received from the Romans, Peroz subjugated the Huns, took many places in their country, and added them to his kingdom. In the end, however, he was taken prisoner by them. When Zeno, emperor of the Romans, heard about it, he sent gold from his own resources, ransomed him, and made peace between him and them. Peroz made a treaty with the Huns that he would not again cross the border of their country to wage war against them. But he went back on his word and broke his treaty, like Zedekiah, and went to war. Like him, he was delivered into the hands of his enemies. His entire army was destroyed and scattered, and he himself was captured alive. In his arrogance, he promised to give thirty mules loaded with coins as a ransom for his life. He sent to the country under his rule and barely managed to gather twenty loads, for he had emptied the entire treasury of the king before him in his earlier wars. As security for these ten additional loads, he left his son Kavadh with them as a hostage and pledge until he sent them. He made an agreement with them twice that he would not wage war again.

When he returned to his kingdom, he imposed a poll tax throughout his land. He sent ten loads of coins and ransomed his son. Once again he gathered an army and went to war. And the words of the prophet who said, “I saw the wicked man rising high like the trees of the forest, but when I passed by, he was gone; I looked for him but could not find him,” were fulfilled in him there in deed. For when battle broke out and the armies clashed with one another, his entire army was destroyed. He himself was sought but could not be found. To this day, no one knows what became of him: whether he was buried beneath the bodies of the slain, whether he threw himself into the sea, whether he hid in the dust of the earth and died of hunger, or whether he concealed himself in the forest and was eaten by wild animals.

During the days of this same Peroz, the Roman Empire was also thrown into turmoil. For the members of the palace household hated Emperor Zeno because he was Isaurian by birth. Basiliscus rebelled against him and became emperor in his place. Later, Zeno prevailed and regained control of his empire. Because he had experienced the hatred that many bore him, he prepared a strong fortress for himself in his homeland, so that if anything bad happened to him, he would have it as a place of refuge. His confidant in this matter was the military commander of Antioch, whose name was Illus, who was himself an Isaurian. For he gave all his fellow countrymen positions of honor and authority, and because of this he was hated all the more by the Romans.

When the fortress had been supplied with everything it needed, and Illus had deposited in it an immense, incalculable amount of gold, he came to the imperial capital to inform Zeno that his wishes had been fulfilled. But Zeno, knowing that he was deceitful and coveted the throne, ordered one of the soldiers to kill him. For many days, the man who had received the order secretly sought [?] to carry out his deed but could not find it. Then he encountered Illus inside the palace, drew his sword, and raised it to strike him. Immediately, one of the soldiers accompanying Illus struck him on the arm with a knife. The sword fell from his hand and cut off Illus's ear. Zeno, to keep his plot against Illus from being exposed, immediately ordered that the soldier be beheaded without questioning. But this very act made Illus suspect all the more that Zeno had given him the order. He got up and departed from there. He went down to Antioch, determined to seek revenge whenever he had the opportunity.

Zeno, who feared Illus because he knew his wickedness, sent men of standing to him in Antioch. He sent word asking him to come up to him, saying that the plot had taken place but that he himself had not wanted to kill him. But he could not soften Illus's stubborn resolve. Illus scorned him and refused to obey his command and go to him. Finally, Zeno sent another military commander against him, whose name was Leontius, with the army under his command. He ordered him to bring Illus up to him by force, and to kill him if he resisted. But when this man arrived in Antioch, Illus corrupted him with gold. And he revealed to him the order he had been given to kill him. When Illus saw that nothing was hidden from him, he too showed him the large amount of gold in his possession, on account of which Zeno wanted to kill him. He persuaded Leontius to join him and rebel with him, also pointing out to him the Romans’ hatred of Zeno. When Leontius was persuaded, Illus was able to reveal his intention. For he could not rebel on his own, nor could he himself become emperor, because the Romans hated him too, on account of his ancestry and his harsh disposition.

Leontius became emperor at Antioch in name, while Illus himself directed affairs. According to some, he was even planning to kill Leontius if they defeated Zeno. A man named Pamprepius, a magician and deceiver, was associated with them. He threw all their affairs into confusion and reversed their fortunes through his deception. To secure the empire for them, he sent envoys to Persia with a large amount of gold, so that the Persians would establish a treaty of friendship with them, or send them an army to help if they needed one. When Zeno heard about what had happened in Antioch, he sent one of his generals, named John, there with a large army.

When the followers of Illus and Leontius heard about the large army coming against them, their hearts trembled. The people of Antioch were also afraid, because they could not endure a siege. They quarreled with them, demanding that they leave the city and, if they could, engage in battle. This alarmed Illus and his followers even more. They planned to leave Antioch and cross the Euphrates River eastward. They sent one of their men, named Matronianus, with five hundred cavalrymen to prepare a royal residence for them in Edessa. But the people of Edessa opposed him and closed the city gates. They guarded the wall as in wartime and did not allow him to enter.

When Illus and his followers heard this, they were forced to engage John in battle. But they could not prevail, because John attacked them forcefully and destroyed most of the army with them. The others scattered, each to his own city. When they could no longer withstand his onslaught, they took those who remained with them and escaped to the fortress I mentioned above as being strongly fortified and well supplied with everything. John pursued them but did not catch them. He encamped [?] around the fortress and kept watch over them. Because they trusted in the strength of the fortress, they allowed the army with them to go down, keeping only the selected and valiant men with them. John vented his anger on those who came down from the fortress, but he could do no harm to Illus and his followers. Besides the natural difficulty of the fortress’s location, it was also remarkably fortified by human workmanship. There was only one road leading up to it, and it was so narrow that two people could not go up it side by side. After a long time, when John had exhausted his stratagems, some of those with Illus and his followers plotted against them, and they were captured while asleep. At Zeno’s command, both of them were killed, along with those who had betrayed them. And the hands of all those who were with them were cut off. Such was the distress among the Romans in the days of Peroz.

After he had been searched for and could not be found, as I said above, his brother Balash became king of the Persians in his place. He was a humble man who loved peace, and he found nothing in the Persian treasury. His land was devastated by the raids of the Huns. For your wisdom is not unaware of the losses and expenses that kings incur in wars, even when they win, let alone when they are defeated. Nor did he receive any help from the Romans, as his brother had. For he sent envoys to Zeno, asking him to send him gold. But because Zeno was preoccupied with the war involving Illus and Leontius, and because he also remembered that the gold they had sent at the beginning of their rebellion had remained there among the Persians, he was unwilling to send him anything. Instead, he wrote to him: “The revenues of Nisibis that you collect are enough for you, for they have rightfully belonged to the Romans for many years now.”

Because Balash had no gold to maintain his troops, he became contemptible in their eyes. The Magi also hated him because he was abolishing their laws and wanted to build bathhouses in the cities for bathing. When they saw that his troops held him in no esteem, they seized him, blinded him, and appointed in his place Kavadh, the son of his brother Peroz, whose name we mentioned above, who had been held as a hostage among the Huns. It was he who stirred up war with the Romans because gold was not given to him. For he sent envoys and one large elephant as a gift to honor the emperor, so that he would send him gold. By the time the envoy reached Antioch in Syria, Zeno had died, and Anastasius had become emperor after him. When the Persian envoy informed his master Kavadh of the change that had taken place in the Roman Empire, he wrote to him, telling him to proceed quickly and ask for the customary gold, or else to tell the emperor to prepare for war.

Instead of speaking words of peace and reconciliation, as he ought to have done, and rejoicing with him at the beginning of the rule that God had newly granted him, he embittered the mind of the faithful emperor Anastasius with threatening words. But when Anastasius heard his arrogant words and learned of his evil ways, and that he had revived the abominable heresy of the Magian religion called that of the Zaradushtakans, which teaches that women should be held in common and that everyone may have sexual relations with whomever he wishes, and that he had mistreated the Armenians under his authority because they would not worship fire, he despised him and did not send him gold. Instead, he wrote to him: “Just as Zeno, who reigned before me, did not send any, neither will I send any until you return Nisibis to me. For my own wars are no small matter either, against the barbarians called Germans, against those called Blemmyes, and against many others. I will not neglect the Roman troops and support yours.”

When the Armenians under Kavadh’s authority heard that no peaceful answer had come to him from the Romans, they took courage and grew strong. They tore down the fire temples that had been built for the Persians in their country and killed the Magi among them. Kavadh sent a marzban against them with an army to punish them and turn them back to worshiping fire. He fought against them, and they destroyed him and his army. They sent envoys to our emperor, offering to submit to him, but he was unwilling to receive them, so that he would not be thought to be provoking war with the Persians. Those, therefore, who blame him for not giving gold should blame the man who demanded what was not his, by force. For if he had asked peacefully and persuasively, it would have been sent to him. But he hardened his mind like Pharaoh and threatened war. But we trust in God's justice, that he will bring upon him an even greater punishment than that [?], because of his filthy laws, since he wanted to corrupt the law of nature and abolish the way of reverence for God.

Furthermore, all the Qadishaye under his authority rebelled against him and wanted to enter Nisibis and establish a king of their own there. He fought against it for no short time. Likewise, the Tamuraye who lived in Persian territory, when they saw that he was giving them nothing, rebelled against him. They relied on the high mountains where they lived. They would come down and plunder and rob the villages around them, the merchants, the travelers, and the local inhabitants, and then go back up. The nobles of his kingdom also hated him, because he had permitted their wives to commit adultery. Likewise, when the Arabs under his authority saw the disorder in his kingdom, they too carried out raids throughout Persian territory, as far as their strength allowed.

At this time another disturbance also arose in Roman territory. For after Zeno's death, the Isaurians rebelled against Emperor Anastasius. They wanted to appoint a king of their own choosing. When Kavadh heard this, he thought he had found his opportunity. He sent envoys to Roman territory, thinking that they would be afraid and send him gold because the Isaurians were rebelling against them. Emperor Anastasius also sent him this message: “If you want it as a loan, I will send it to you. But if it is a matter of customary payment, I will not let the Roman armies be worn down in the war against the Isaurians while I become a helper to the Persians.” These words humbled Kavadh's pride, because his plan had not succeeded. The Isaurians were defeated, destroyed, and killed, and all their cities were demolished and burned. The Persian nobles secretly planned to kill Kavadh because of his impure conduct and perverse laws. When he learned of this, he abandoned his kingdom and fled to the land of the Huns, to the king with whom he had been brought up while he was a hostage.

His brother Jamasp became king over the Persians in his place. Kavadh himself took a wife in the land of the Huns who was his sister's daughter. His sister had been taken captive there in the battle in which his father was killed. Because she was a king's daughter, she became the wife of the king of the Huns. He had a daughter by her, and when Kavadh fled there, she gave her to him as his wife. Now that he had the confidence that came from becoming the king's son-in-law, he wept before him every day, asking him to give him an army to help him, so that he could go and kill the nobles and establish himself over his kingdom. His father-in-law gave him a considerable army, as he had asked. When he approached Persian territory, his brother heard of it and withdrew before him. Those who would not submit to him willingly were about to be defeated in battle. But if they would serve as his soldiers, they would enter Roman territory with him, and from the plunder there he would give them everything they had been deprived of. They, however, feared the army of the Huns and surrendered to him. When the Cadiseni who were encamped near Nisibis heard this, they too submitted. When the Arabs learned that he was preparing to wage war against the Romans, they gathered around him with great enthusiasm. The Armenians, however, were unwilling to obey him because of those fire temples they had previously demolished. So he gathered an army and fought against them. When he had overpowered them, he did not lay waste to them, but promised them that he would not even force them to worship fire, provided they would help him in the war against the Romans. Out of fear they agreed, though unwillingly. As for what Kavadh did before entering Roman territory, I will tell you about it at the proper time. But now, since you also instructed me to write about the signs and punishments that occurred in their time, and about the locusts, and about the locusts, and about the pestilence and high prices—and these came earlier in time—I turn my account to them. So that the narrative will not be confused, I am setting down the years separately, one by one, and under each year I will write separately what happened in it, with God as my helper through the support of the prayers of Your Excellency.

The year 806 of Alexander. Concerning the cause of the war, then, and how it was stirred up, I believe I have informed you sufficiently, our father, although I wrote these accounts briefly because I wished to avoid a lengthy narrative. Some of them I found in old books, and some I learned through meeting men who had served as envoys to both kings. Others I learned from people who had themselves been involved in these events. But now I wish to tell you about what happened among us, because this year marked the beginning of the severe punishments and the signs that occurred in our days.

At this time health prevailed throughout our country, but the pains and diseases of our souls were many. But God, who desires sinners to turn from their sins and live, made our body a mirror for us. He filled our whole body with sores, so that through our outward condition he might show us what our inward condition was like. Through the blemishes of our bodies we could learn how ugly the blemishes of our souls were. And just as everyone had sinned, everyone was struck by this affliction. For swellings and eruptions appeared on all the inhabitants of our city. Many people's faces became swollen and filled with pus, making a terrifying sight. Others had their whole bodies covered with sores or pustules, even the palms of their hands and the soles of their feet. Others had large open sores on individual limbs. And others had large open sores appearing on individual limbs. But through the grace of God that sheltered them, the disease did not remain with anyone for long, nor did any deformity or damage develop in the body. Rather, although the scars of the wounds remained visible after recovery, the limbs were left intact, able to perform their necessary functions in the body. At this time in Edessa, thirty measures of wheat were sold for one dinar, and barley at [?] measures.

The year 807. On the seventeenth day of the month of Iyar in this year, while good things were being sent abundantly from heaven to all people, and the crops were plentiful through blessing, and rain was falling, and the fruits of the earth were growing in their season, most of the city's inhabitants had abandoned hope of life and were openly practicing wickedness. While they reveled in arrogance, they did not even offer thanksgiving for God's gifts. Instead, in confidence arising from [?] they lived, and they were being corrupted by the diseases of sin. When the secret and open sins in which they occupied themselves were not enough for them, they made preparations on this specified day, which was Friday, the eve of the Sabbath, for a dancer to perform on it. It is called the Trimerion. Countless lamps were lit in honor of this festival, although this custom had not previously existed in the city. From the gate of the theater to the Gate of the Arches, they were arranged on the ground beside the river. Lighted lamps were placed along its bank. They were also hung in the porticoes, in the Antiphorus, on the upper terraces, and in many other places. Because of this wickedness, a miraculous sign from God occurred to rebuke them. The emblem of the cross that the statue of the blessed Emperor Constantine held in its hand moved about one cubit away from the statue's hand. It remained like this on Friday and Saturday until evening. On Sunday, the emblem came back of its own accord and approached its place. The statue held it in its hand, just as it had held it before. Through this sign, discerning people understood that the practice that had been carried out was far removed from God's will.

The year 808. This sign from above was not enough to make us refrain from wickedness. Instead, we hurried all the more and readily approached sinful acts. The lowly slandered their companions, and the powerful were full of favoritism. Envy and deceit gained control over us all. Adultery and sexual immorality increased. The disease of sores grew more severe among people, and the eyes of many were damaged, both in the city and in the villages. A worthy zeal arose in Bishop Mar Cyrus, and he urged the city's inhabitants to make a silver litter in honor of the vessels of the mysteries, so that they could be placed in it whenever people went to celebrate the service with them at the commemoration of one of the martyrs. Everyone gave whatever they could afford. Eutychianus, Aurina's husband, was the first to show his goodwill, and he gave hundreds of dinars from his own resources.

The governor Anastasius was relieved of his office, and Alexander came in his place at the end of this year. He cleared the city's streets of refuse and removed the benches that had been built for the craftsmen in the porticoes and streets. He placed a chest in front of his headquarters, made a hole in its lid, and wrote above it: “Anyone who wishes to report something but finds it difficult to do so openly should write it down and put it inside without fear.” Through this means he learned about many matters, because many people wrote things down and put them into it. He regularly sat every Friday in the martyrs’ shrine of Saint John the Baptist and Saint Addai the apostle. He settled lawsuits without anyone suffering loss. The oppressed gained strength against their oppressors, and those who had been robbed against their robbers. They brought their cases to him, and he judged them. Even cases more than fifty years old that had not been pursued were brought before him and settled. He built the [?] near the Gate of the Rocks. He also began building a bathhouse that had been planned years earlier for construction beside the grain storehouse. He ordered the craftsmen to hang crosses over their shops on Saturday evenings, with five lamps shining on them.

The year eight hundred and nine. While these things were happening, the time again arrived for the festival at which pagan tales are sung. The citizens devoted even more attention to it than they had before. For seven days beforehand, they would come up together from the theater in the evening, wearing linen garments, clothed in patterned robes, with their belts undone and lamps shining before them. They burned incense in braziers, stayed awake all night, and went around the city praising the dancer until morning, with singing, shouting, and revelry. On these pretexts they even neglected going to prayer, and no one gave a thought to calamity. Instead, they arrogantly mocked the modesty of their fathers, saying, “They did not know how to do these things as we do.” They would say, “The people who lived in the city in earlier times were uncultured and ignorant.” Thus they eagerly pursued wickedness, and there was no one to correct, rebuke, or admonish them. Although Xenaias, bishop of Mabbug, had been welcomed in Edessa, a man who, more than others, is thought to have undertaken the task of laboring at teaching, he did not speak to them about this matter for more than one day. But God, in his mercy, clearly showed them his concern for them, so that they would stop their wrongdoing. For two basilicas and the warm room of the summer bathhouse collapsed, and by God’s grace no one was injured there, although there were many people in it, working inside and outside. None of them died except two men who were crushed at the doorway of the bathhouse as they fled from the sound of the collapse. As they clung to the door on its two sides, pulling it this way and that to turn it, they delayed over a dispute about which of them would go out first. Stones fell on them, and they died. But all sensible people thanked God for sparing the city the mourning of many people. For that bathhouse was due to open for bathing within a few days. It collapsed so completely that even its lowest stones, which had been laid at ground level, were torn from their places.

In this same year, an order came from Emperor [?] that the gold payment which craftsmen made once every four years should be abolished and that they should be freed from the tax. This order came not only to Edessa but to all the cities under Roman rule. The people of Edessa had been paying one hundred and forty pounds of gold once every four years. The whole city rejoiced, and everyone, from the greatest to the least, dressed in white. He carried burning candles and fragrant censers, and they went out with psalms and hymns, thanking God and praising the emperor. To the martyrs’ shrine of Saint Sergius and Saint Simeon. They offered the Eucharist there and entered the city, and he held a festival of joy and enjoyment throughout the week. They established that they would celebrate this festival every year. All the craftsmen reclined and enjoyed themselves, company by company, in the church courtyard and in all the city’s porticoes.

In this same year, on the fifth day of June, Bishop Cyrus departed from this world, and Peter succeeded him. He added the feast of Palm Sunday to the year’s festivals. He also established the custom of consecrating water during the night before the feast of Epiphany. And concerning the oil of anointing on Thursdays [?] before all the people, along with the rest of the other festivals. Alexander the governor was dismissed, and Demosthenes succeeded him. At his command, all the porticoes of our city were whitewashed. Those who had experience of such matters were greatly distressed by this. For they said that it was a sign [?] of things soon to happen in the country.

The year eight hundred and ten. At this time a demonstration of God’s justice was revealed against us, to put an end to our evil conduct. In May of this year, when the day arrived on which that wicked pagan festival was to be celebrated, a great swarm of locusts came into our country from the south. During that year among us, it neither did harm nor caused damage, but only laid its eggs in our country in great quantities. While its eggs lay planted in the ground, powerful tremors were occurring on the earth. It is clear that these were occurring to awaken humanity from its immersion in sin, so that it would not be chastised by famine and pestilence.

In August of this same year, an order came from Emperor Anastasius: [?] wild-beast shows in the cities of the Roman Empire. In September there was a powerful earthquake, and a loud sound from heaven was heard on earth. The earth was shaken from its foundations by that sound, and all the villages and cities felt the sound and the earthquake. Alarming reports and bad news came to us from every direction. According to what some people said, an astonishing sign appeared in the Euphrates River and at the hot spring of Abarna: The flow of their sources ceased on that very day. I do not think this is false, because the earth is often split open by earthquakes. It happens that even the waters flowing in places that split open are stopped in their course, and sometimes they are diverted in another direction. Likewise, the blessed David, when speaking in the eighteenth psalm about the punishments that came from God upon his enemies through the shaking of the earth, the upheaval of mountains, and other such things, makes known that this too happened. For he says, “The springs of water were laid bare, and the foundations of the world were revealed at your rebuke, Lord.” A letter also arrived during this same month and was read before the whole congregation of the church, saying that the city of Nicopolis had suddenly collapsed at midnight and had trapped within it all its inhabitants, as well as the strangers who were there. And of the brothers from our schools who used to travel there, those who were inside it were buried there. Their companions who returned told us about it. For the entire circuit of the city wall, and everything within it, collapsed that night, and none of them remained alive except the city's bishop and two other men, who had been sleeping behind the chancel of the church's sanctuary. When the roof of the building in which they were sleeping fell, one end of its timbers rested against the sanctuary wall, and it did not bury them. A brother who loves the truth told me this: “At evening on the night when it collapsed, a companion and I were eating inside it. He became uneasy and said to me, ‘Get up! Let us go out and spend the night outside the city, in that hollow where we usually stay, because I cannot spend the night here. The air feels oppressive to me, and I cannot get to sleep.’ So he and I got up, went outside the city, and spent the night in that hollow, as we usually did. When dawn was approaching, I woke the brother who was with me and said to him, ‘Get up, for day has broken. Let us go into the city and attend to our business.’ He and I got up and came to the city, and we found all its buildings overturned, with people and livestock, oxen and camels buried there. The sound of their groaning came up from beneath the ground.” Those who gathered there brought the bishop out from beneath those timbers (of the roof) under which he had been sheltered. He was asking for bread and wine with which they could celebrate the sacrament, because the whole city had been overturned and nothing in it was left standing. By chance, he met a blessed traveler, who gave him small pieces of bread and a little wine. He presented the offering and prayed, and gave those who were there communion in the sacrament of life. At that time, I think, he resembled righteous Lot when he escaped from Sodom. Let this much suffice.

There was also in that northern region a shrine of the martyrs called the shrine of Arsamosata. It was solidly built and beautifully adorned. On the appointed day when the saints laid to rest there were commemorated each year, many people gathered there from every direction, some for prayer and others for trade. For the gathering held there provided a substantial livelihood for people. While a great crowd was there—men, women, and children, of every height and size—there were powerful flashes of lightning and violent thunderclaps, and the sounds of an earthquake. Everyone fled into that shrine of the martyrs to seek refuge with the bones of the blessed ones. While they were in great fear and were standing in prayer and worship at midnight, that shrine of the martyrs collapsed and crushed beneath it most of the people who were inside. This happened on the very day when Nicopolis fell.

The year 811. Yet through all these earthquakes and disasters, not one of us stopped doing evil. Our region and our city were left without respite, because they were reserved for further chastisement. And because reports from far away did not frighten us, we suffered a wound for which there is no cure. Let us therefore acknowledge God's justice and say: “The Lord is righteous, and his judgments are entirely just.” For even now, in his patience, he wishes to restrain us from our evil deeds through signs and wonders. In October of this year, on the twenty-third, a Saturday, at sunrise, the sun's light was snatched away from it, and its luminous disk became like silver. It had no visible rays, and our eyes could look at it easily, without hindrance. For it had no brilliance, flashes, or rays to prevent our eyes from looking at it. Rather, just as it is easy for us to look at the moon, so we could also look at it. It remained like this until about [?] hours. The earth, on which the little light that remained was shining, looked pale, as though ashes or sulfur had been scattered over it. On this same day, another terrifying and dreadful sign occurred in the city wall. This city, because of its king's faith and the righteousness of its inhabitants in former times, had been deemed worthy to receive a blessing from our Lord. It now came close to destroying its present inhabitants because of their many sins. For a breach appeared in the wall south of the Great Gate, and some of the stones from that spot were scattered a considerable distance away. At the command of our father, Bishop Peter, prayers of supplication were held, and everyone begged God for mercy. For he led out the entire community of male and female ascetics, together with all the members of the holy church, rich and poor, men, women, and children. Carrying crosses, they went around through all the city's streets with psalms and hymns, dressed in black garments of humility. All the monasteries in our region also kept their services with great diligence. Through the prayers of all the holy ones, the sun's light was restored to its proper state, and we received a little encouragement.

In November we saw three signs in the sky at midday. One of them was in the middle of the sky, on the southern side. Its color resembled that of the rainbow that appears in the clouds, and its curve faced upward—that is, its rounded part was below and its ends above. Another was in the east, and another in the west. Then, in January, we saw another sign in the southwest, right in that corner of the sky. It resembled a lance. Some people said that it was a broom of destruction, while others said that it was a lance of war.

Up to this point we were being admonished by reports and signs. But from this point onward, who can describe the distress that surrounded our region on every side? In March of this year, locusts came up against us from the ground. They were so numerous that we thought it was not only the brood already in the ground that had emerged against us, but that the air itself was spewing them out upon us, and that they were also descending upon us from heaven. While they were still crawling, they devoured and consumed the whole region of Arab, and all the territories of Reshaina, Tella, and Edessa. Once they took flight, their swarms stretched from the border of Assyria to the western sea. It went north as far as the border of Beth Urta. It devoured and devastated these regions, consuming everything in them. Thus, even before war broke out, we could see with our own eyes what was said about the Babylonian: “Before him the land is like the garden of Eden, and behind him a desolate wilderness.” Had the Lord’s command not restrained it, it would have devoured people and animals, as we heard it had done in one of the villages. Some people had laid a small infant in a field while they were working. While they were going from one end of the field to the other, it swooped down on him and deprived him of life. Immediately, in the month of Nisan, grain and everything else began to grow expensive. Four modii of wheat were being sold for a dinar. In the months of Haziran and Tammuz, the inhabitants of these regions were trying to survive and sowing millet to meet their needs, but it did not suffice for them. For it did not thrive. As the year was drawing to its close, misery from hunger surrounded the people, and they sold their possessions for half their value: livestock, cattle, sheep, and pigs. For the locusts had devoured the entire crop and left neither pasture nor food, either for people or for animals. Many abandoned their own regions and moved to other regions in the north and west. Those who were weak in the villages, the elderly and the children, the women and the infants, and those so afflicted by hunger that they could not walk and travel to distant regions, went into the cities to beg and stay alive. Many villages and estates were emptied of people. But even those who went to distant regions did not escape punishment. Rather, as it is written about the people of Israel, wherever they went out, the hand of the Lord was against them for harm. The same thing happened to them. For plague struck them in the regions to which they had gone. Those who entered Edessa were likewise overtaken by plague, which I shall describe shortly, as well as I can. But I think no one can describe it as it actually happened.

Now I shall write to you about the high prices, as you asked me, for I had not intended to record anything about this. But I am forcing myself to do so, lest you think I have disregarded your instruction. At this time wheat was being sold at four modii of wheat for a dinar, and barley at six. Chickpeas cost five hundred nummi a qab, vetches four hundred nummi a qab, and lentils three hundred and sixty nummi a qab. Meat, however, had not yet become expensive. But as time went on, prices kept rising, and the suffering caused by hunger grew more severe among the people. Everything that could not be eaten became cheap—clothes, utensils, and household goods— with possessions being sold for half or a third of their value. Yet they did not suffice to feed their owners, because bread was so expensive. At this time our father, Mar Peter, journeyed to the emperor to ask him to remit the tax. But the governor seized the village landowners, subjected them to severe pressure, and demanded payment from them. While the bishop was pleading with the emperor, gold was sent by the governor to the imperial capital. When the emperor saw that the gold had reached him, he was unwilling to remit the tax. But so as not to send our father away empty-handed, Bifilas remitted the payments that the villagers had been making, and exempted the city's inhabitants from drawing water for the Romans.

The governor himself then set out for the emperor, wearing his sword. He left Eusebius to take his place and administer the city. When this Eusebius saw that the bakers could not produce enough bread for the market because of the great number of villagers who had filled the city, and because of the poor who had no bread in their homes, he ordered that anyone who wished could make bread and sell it in the market. Jewish women came, and he gave them wheat from the storehouse. They made bread for the market. Even so, the poor remained in distress, because they had no money with which to buy bread. They went around the markets, porticoes, and courtyards, begging for a scrap of bread. No one had bread to spare at home. Whenever one of them obtained some coins and could not [?] buy bread with them, he would use them to buy himself turnips, cabbage, or mallows. He would eat them raw. This caused vegetables to become expensive and brought about a shortage of everything in the city and the villages. Such was the situation. People rushed into the holy places and, because of their hunger, ate the consecrated bread as though it were ordinary bread. Others cut pieces from dead bodies that were unfit to eat, cooked them, and ate them. Your own trustworthiness bears witness to these things.

The year eight hundred and twelve. In this year, after the grape harvest, wine was sold at six measures for a dinar, and a qab of hempseed for three hundred nummi. The famine grew severe in the villages and the city. Those who remained in the villages were eating bitter vetch. Others roasted [?] and ate it, though they did not have enough even of that to satisfy their hunger. Those in the city wandered through the markets, picking up vegetable roots and leaves that had fallen among the rubbish, and eating them. They slept in the porticoes and markets, and howled night and day from the torment of hunger. Their bodies wasted away, and they became gaunt. They looked like ghosts because their bodies were so thin. The whole city was full of them, and they began dying in the porticoes and markets.

When Demosthenes the governor went up to the emperor, he told him about this distress. The emperor gave him a considerable amount of gold to distribute to the poor. When he returned from the emperor to Edessa, he marked many of them with lead tags around their necks, and gave each of them a pound of bread a day. But they could not survive, because they were suffering from the torment of the hunger that had wasted them away. The death toll rose sharply at this time, in the month of November. Then, in the month of December, when frost and ice began to form, the sleep of death overtook them as they slept, because they spent the night in the porticoes and markets. Children and infants cried out in all our markets. Some of their mothers had died, while others had abandoned them and fled when they asked for food, because they had nothing to give them. Naked corpses lay in all our markets. The city's inhabitants could not keep up with burying them. While they were carrying out those who had died first, they would find others as soon as they returned. While Mar Nonnus was in charge of the hospital, the brothers would go around afterward and gather up these bodies. The whole city would gather at the hospital gate, and they would go out and bury them from one morning to the next. The stewards of the church also took part: Mar Tuthael the priest and Mar Stratonicus, who was later raised to the rank of bishop in the city of Harran. They set up a shelter in the buildings of the church of Edessa. Those who were suffering would enter and take refuge there. Many bodies were found in the shelter, and they buried them together with those from the hospital.

The governor removed the doors of the basilicas near the winter baths and spread straw and mats there. People slept there, but there was not enough room for them. When the city's leading men saw this, they too set up shelters, and many people went in and found refuge in them. The Romans also prepared places where the sick could sleep, and they provided for their expenses. They were dying continually and painfully. Although many of them were buried every day, their numbers kept increasing. For word had spread through the countryside around the city that the people of Edessa cared for those in need. For this reason, a countless multitude of people entered the city. The bathhouse below the Church of the Apostles, near the Great Gate, was also full of sick people. Many bodies were carried out of it every day. The whole city was eager to gather together and accompany those who were being carried out of the hospital, with psalms, praises, hymns, and songs full of hope in the resurrection. The women, too, accompanied them with bitter weeping and loud cries. At their head walked the diligent shepherd Mar Peter. The judge and all the nobles were also with them. Once these people had been buried, everyone would return and accompany the dead from his own neighborhood. When the burial places belonging to the hospital and the church were full, the governor went out and opened the old tombs near the Church of Mar Qona, which earlier generations had built with great effort. They filled these, and then opened others, but these too were not enough for them. In the end, they opened and filled every old tomb there was. For more than a hundred bodies were carried out of the hospital every day, and on many days a hundred and twenty, or even a hundred and thirty, from the beginning of November to the end of March. At that time, throughout all the streets of the city, nothing could be heard except weeping for the dead or the cries of those in agony. Many people also died in the church courtyards, in the courtyards of the city, and in the inns. They also died along the roads as they came to enter the city. In February, prices rose still further and the death toll increased. Wheat sold at thirteen qabs for a dinar, barley at eighteen qabs, and a pound of meat for a hundred nummi. A pound of chicken cost three hundred nummi, and an egg forty nummi. In short, everything edible was expensive.

In March, prayers were offered that the deadly plague among the strangers might be stopped. As the inhabitants of the city pleaded on their behalf, they resembled blessed David when he spoke to the angel who was destroying his people. For if I have sinned and acted foolishly, what sin have these innocent sheep committed? Let your hand be against me and against my father’s household. In the month of Nisan, the plague began among the inhabitants of the city. Many biers were being carried out each day, and no one could keep count of them. This devastation by plague occurred not only in Edessa, but throughout the region from Antioch to Nisibis. Thus people were being destroyed and tormented by famine and plague. Many of the rich, who were not suffering from hunger, also died. Many of the city’s leading men also died that year. In the months of Haziran and Tammuz, after the harvest, we hoped that we would now find relief from the high prices. But our expectations were not fulfilled as we had hoped. Instead, wheat from the new harvest was selling at only five modii for a dinar.

The year eight hundred and thirteen. After these afflictions of locusts, famine, and plague, about which I have written to you, we were given a little respite through God’s mercy, so that we could endure the things to come, as we learned from the events themselves. For there was an abundant grape harvest, and wine was sold straight from the winepress at twenty-five measures for a dinar. The poor were sustained from the vineyards by the crop of raisins. For the farmers and laborers said that the crop of raisins was more abundant than the wheat crop. For a hot wind arose when the grapes were beginning to ripen, and most of them dried up. Discerning people said that this had happened through the providence of God, the Lord of all, and that this event was mercy mingled with chastisement, so that the villagers could sustain themselves with these raisins and not perish from hunger as they had the previous year. For even at this time, wheat was selling at only four modii for a dinar, and barley at six. Such a sign of mercy, then, occurred during the months of Tishri. The whole winter of that year was also exceptionally rainy. In various places, the seed that had been sown grew taller than a man, even before Nisan had arrived. Even the plowed land yielded only a little less than the land that had been sown. Likewise, the roofs of houses sprouted a great deal of grass. Some people cut this and sold it as though it were grass from the fields. Because it had awns and was fully grown, its buyers did not recognize it. That year too, we were waiting and hoping that grain would become very cheap, as in former years. But this expectation was not fulfilled. For in the month of Iyar, a scorching wind blew for three days and scorched all the grain in our region, except in a few small places.

In this same month, when the day arrived on which that wicked festival of Greek myths was celebrated, about which we gave information above, an order came from Emperor Anastasius that the dancers were no longer to dance in any city within the territory of his empire. Anyone who considers how events turned out will therefore not blame us for saying that because of the wickedness practiced by the city’s inhabitants at that festival, the punishments of famine and plague came upon us one after another. For before thirty days had passed after it was abolished, wheat that had been selling at six modii for a dinar was being sold at twenty-two. And it became clear to everyone that God can, if he wills, bless even a small harvest and give enough food to satisfy those who repent of their sins. For although all the grain had withered, as I said, all this abundance came within thirty days from the little that remained. But perhaps someone will still say, “You have not judged correctly. This repentance was not voluntary, so that mercy should be shown on its account.” For it was the emperor who forcibly abolished the festival by ordering that the dancers should not dance at all. But we say that God, because of his abundant goodness, was looking for a reason to show mercy even to those who were unworthy. We have proof in the mercy he showed Ahab when he was cowed by Elijah’s rebuke: he did not bring upon him during his lifetime the disaster that had already been decreed against his household. But I am not saying that this was the only sin being practiced in our city. For many sins are committed both secretly and openly. And because the governors also share in them, I did not want to name the sins explicitly, lest I give those who like to find fault a reason to say about us that I am speaking against the rulers. But so as not to leave the matter entirely concealed, since I also promised above to tell you why war was stirred up against us, and so as not to say anything further about these shameless people, I set down the prophet’s words, from which you may understand. When he saw his fellow countrymen engaging in practices like those carried on today in our city, and especially among you and throughout the whole district, he said to them as if from the mouth of the Lord, “Woe to the one who says to a father, ‘What are you begetting?’ and to a woman, ‘What are you conceiving?’” As for the rest of these matters, it is better to remain silent. For it is right to obey the words of Scripture, which say, “Let the prudent person keep silent at such a time, because it is an evil time.” But if our Lord grants that we see you in good health, we will speak with you about these things as best we can.

Now hear about the disasters that occurred in this year and the sign that appeared on the day they occurred, since you also asked us about this. On the twenty-second day of the month of August of this year, on the night before Friday, a great fire appeared to us, blazing in the northern region throughout the night. We thought that it was about to sweep away the whole earth that night in a flood of fire. But the mercy of our Lord kept us unharmed. A letter was sent to us by some acquaintances who were traveling to Jerusalem. It contained the following: On the night when that great blazing fire appeared, the city of Ptolemais, which is Acre, was overthrown, and nothing in it was left standing. Then, some days later, people from Tyre and Sidon came to us and told us that on the day when the fire appeared and Ptolemais was overthrown, when the fire appeared and Ptolemais was overthrown, on that very day half of each of their cities collapsed—that is, half of Tyre and half of Sidon. In Berytus, too, only the Jewish synagogue collapsed, on that very day when Acre was overthrown. The people of Nicomedia, however, were handed over to Satan to be chastised. Many of them were tormented by demons until they remembered the words of our Lord, devoted themselves to fasting and prayer, and received healing.

Also Kavadh, son of Peroz, king of the Persians, on this very day when that fire appeared. He gathered the entire Persian army, marched north, and entered Roman territory. With the army of Huns that accompanied him, he laid siege to Theodosiopolis in Armenia and captured it within a few days. For the governor of that region, whose name was Constantine, had rebelled against the Romans and surrendered it to him because of some hostility he had toward the emperor. Kavadh therefore plundered the city, devastated it, and burned it. He also destroyed all the villages in the northern region. He carried off the remaining survivors into captivity and made Constantine his military commander. He left a garrison in Theodosiopolis and departed from there.

The year 814. In this year great afflictions also descended upon the land of Mesopotamia, where we live. Thus the things that Christ our Lord decreed concerning Jerusalem in his Gospel and fulfilled in deed, and also the things spoken concerning the end of this world, apply as well to what has happened to us at this time. For after earthquakes had occurred in various places, as I wrote to you, and after there had been famines and plagues, and terrors and alarms, and great signs had appeared from heaven, nation rose against nation and kingdom against kingdom. We fell by the edge of the sword and were carried captive to every land. Our land was trampled by foreign nations, so that, were it not for the words of our Lord, who said, “When you hear of wars and disturbances, do not be afraid, for these things must happen first, but the end has not yet come,” we would have dared to say that the end of the world had arrived. Indeed, many thought and said this. But we observed that this war was not taking place throughout the whole world. Along with this, we also remembered the words of the blessed Paul, in which he warned the Thessalonians concerning the coming of our Lord, saying that they should not be alarmed by a spoken message, by a spirit, or by a misleading letter supposedly from him, claiming that the day of the Lord was already at hand. He explained that the end could not come until the false Christ was revealed. From these words of our Lord and his apostle, therefore, we understood that these things had happened to us not because this was the final age, but to discipline us, because our sins had grown great.

For Kavadh, king of the Persians, came from the north on the fifth day of October, a Saturday, and laid siege to the city of Amida, which is here in our land of Mesopotamia. He came with his entire army. But when Anastasius, emperor of the Romans, heard that Kavadh had assembled his army, he did not wish to confront him in battle, so that blood would not be shed on either side. Instead, he sent him gold through Rufinus and instructed him that if Kavadh was still at the frontier and had not yet crossed into Roman territory, he should give him the gold and send him away. But when Rufinus reached Caesarea in Cappadocia, he heard that Kavadh had devastated Ingilene, Sophene, Armenia, and Arabia. He left the gold in Caesarea and went to him. He told him to withdraw from the territory and receive the gold. But Kavadh refused. Instead, he seized Rufinus and ordered that he be kept under guard. He and his entire army attacked Amida with every kind of warfare, day and night, and he built a siege mound against it. The people of Amida also built, adding to the height of the wall. When the siege mound had been raised, the Persians brought forward the head of the battering ram. When they struck the wall repeatedly, that new structure gave way, because it had not yet settled, and it fell. But the people of Amida opened a breach in the wall beneath the siege mound and secretly dragged the earth piled in it into the city, supporting the structure with upright posts. The siege mound was undermined and collapsed.

When Kavad could not overcome the city's strength, he sent Nu'man, king of the Arabs, with his entire army to go south into the territory of Harran. Some of the Persian army also advanced ahead of them as far as the city of Constantina, which is Tella. They plundered, looted, and devastated the whole region. On the nineteenth day of that same month of November, Olympius, the military commander of Tella, and Eugenius, the military commander of Melitene, who had come down at that time, went out, together with their troops, and slaughtered the Persians they found in the villages around Tella. They turned back to return to the city. Someone informed them that there were five hundred men in a certain valley, not very far from them. They prepared to go against them. The Roman troops with them had scattered to strip the slain. Because it was night, Olympius ordered a fire to be lit on the top of a hill, and horns to be blown so that those who had scattered would gather around them. But the Persian commanders who were encamped in the village of Tell Bashme, when they saw the glow of the fire and heard the sound of the horns, armed their entire force and came against them. When the Roman cavalry saw that the Persians outnumbered them, they turned back. But the infantry could not escape and were forced to fight. They gathered and drew up for battle. They formed what is called a chelone, that is, a tortoise formation, and fought for a long time. When the Persian force became too strong for them, and Huns and Arabs also joined the attack against them, their ranks were broken and they were thrown into confusion among one another. They became mixed in among the cavalry, and in the dust raised by the Arabs' horses they were trampled and crushed. Many of the Romans were slaughtered, and the rest were taken captive.

On the twenty-sixth day of this same month, Nu'man also came from the south and entered the territory of Harran, laying waste and [?]. He carried off the people, livestock, and possessions of the whole territory of Harran. He even came as far as Edessa, devastating and plundering all the villages and taking their inhabitants captive. The number of people he led into captivity was eighteen thousand five hundred, besides those who were killed, and besides the livestock, possessions, and plunder of every kind. The reason all these people were found in the villages was that it was grape-harvest time. For not only did the villagers go out for the grape harvest, but many people from Harran and Edessa had also gone out and were taken captive. Because of these events, Edessa was shut up and kept under guard. Trenches were dug, the wall was repaired, and the city gates were reinforced with metal plates, because they were worn out. They wanted to renew them and make barriers for the river's sluice gates, lest anyone enter through them. There was not enough iron to be found for the work, so an order was issued that every household in Edessa should provide ten pounds of iron. When this had been done, the work was completed. But when Eugenius saw that he could not defeat all the Persians, He led the troops he had left, marched against the garrison stationed there, and captured the city.

Kavadh, meanwhile, was still fighting against Amida. He persisted in his efforts to raise the siege mound that had collapsed. He ordered the Persians to fill it with stones and timber, and to bring fabrics of hair, wool, and linen and make them into panniers or sacks, fill them with earth, and build them up above the mound he had made, so that it could quickly be raised to the height of the wall. Then the people of Amida assembled a machine that the Persians themselves nicknamed “the Butcher,” because it frustrated all their efforts and caused them destruction. For with this machine the people of Amida hurled enormous stones, each weighing more than three hundred pounds. In this way the covering of raw wool beneath which the Persians sheltered was torn apart, and those standing beneath it were slaughtered. The head of the battering ram was also broken by the constant barrage of stones, which were hurled without a pause. For the people of Amida could not inflict as much damage on the Persians with anything else as they could with these enormous stones. The covering of raw wool was laid in many layers, and the Persians poured water over it. Arrows could not damage it because of its thickness, nor could fire because of its wetness. But these enormous stones hurled from the Butcher destroyed the covering, the men, and their weapons. Thus the Persians were defeated and gave up trying to ascend by that mound. They decided to return to their own country. For during the three months they had besieged the city, fifty thousand of them had perished in the battles fought every day, by night and by day. But the people of Amida became confident in their victory and grew careless. They no longer guarded the wall as diligently as before. On the tenth day of January, the guards on the wall drank a great deal of wine because of the bitter cold. When night came, they lay down and sank into a deep sleep. Others abandoned their posts because rain was falling, and went down to shelter in their houses. Whether, then, it was through this negligence, as we believe, or through a treacherous scheme of betrayal, as some people say, or through punishment from God, the Persians gained control of Amida’s wall by means of ladders, although the gates had not been opened and the wall had not been breached. They devastated the city and plundered its possessions. Kavadh trampled on its holy things, dishonored its worship, stripped its churches, and led its inhabitants away into captivity, except for the elderly, the infirm, and those who had hidden themselves. They left a garrison of three thousand men there, and all the rest went down to Mount Sinjar. So that the Persians who remained would not be troubled by the smell of the bodies of the people of Amida, they carried them out and piled them into two heaps outside the northern gate. The number of those carried out through the northern gate was more than eighty thousand, apart from those whom they brought out alive and stoned outside the city, and apart from those whom they stabbed on top of the mound they had built, and apart from those whom they threw into the Tigris, and those who died in all the various ways whose deaths we cannot recount.

Then Kavadh released Rufinus to go and tell the emperor what had happened. Everywhere he went, Rufinus recounted these atrocities. At this news, the cities east of the Euphrates were alarmed and prepared to flee westward. Now the respected Jacob, the ecclesiastical visitor, who had composed many discourses on passages of Scripture and had written poems and songs about the time of the locusts, did not neglect, even at this time, what was fitting for him. Instead, he wrote letters of admonition to all the cities, encouraging them to trust in God's deliverance and urging them not to flee. When Emperor Anastasius heard, he too sent a large Roman force to spend the winter in those cities and guard them. But Kavadh was not satisfied with all the plunder he had taken and the captives he had carried off, nor had he had enough of the great amount of blood he had shed. Instead, he sent envoys to the emperor, saying, “Send me gold.” The emperor did not send any, but prepared to take revenge and exact retribution for those [?] who had perished. In the month of May, he sent three army commanders against him: Areobindus, Patricius, and Hypatius, with many officers accompanying them. Areobindus went down and camped on the frontier near Dara and Ammoudin, opposite the city of Nisibis. He had twelve thousand men with him. Patricius and Hypatius camped against Amida to drive the Persian garrison out of it. They had forty thousand men with them. At this time Apion the prefect also went down and stayed in Edessa to oversee provisions for the Roman army accompanying them. Because the bakers could not produce enough bread, he ordered wheat to be given to every household in Edessa, so that they could make hardtack at their own expense. On the first occasion, the people of Edessa supplied six hundred and thirty thousand measures.

When Kavadh saw how few men Areobindus had, he sent against them the force he had with him at Singara [?], twenty thousand Persians. Areobindus pursued them once and then a second time, until they were driven back to the gate of Nisibis, suffering slaughter. Many of the fugitives were crushed to death at the gate as they crowded in. In the month of July, Huns and Arabs also assembled with the Persians to come against him, with Constantine at their head. When he learned this from scouts, he sent Calliopius of Aleppo to Patricius and Hypatius, saying, “Come to me and help me, because a large army is about to come against us.” But they did not listen. Instead, they remained in their positions near Amida [?]. When the Persians came against Areobindus and his men, he was unable to fight them. Instead, he abandoned their camp and escaped to Tella and Edessa. All their equipment was plundered and carried off.

Meanwhile, the men under Patricius and Hypatius were assembling three wooden towers by which to climb onto the wall of Amida. When the towers had been completed at great expense and reinforced with iron so that nothing could damage them, news reached them of what had happened on the frontier. They burned the towers, left that place, and went after the Persians, but did not catch them. One of the officers, named Pharzman, and another named Theodore used a ruse: they sent a flock of sheep to pass near Amida [?]. They and their troops lay in ambush. When the Persians inside Amida saw the sheep, about four hundred picked men came out to seize them. The Romans who were lying in ambush rose up, routed them, and captured their leader alive. He promised them that he would hand Amida over to them. For this reason Patricius and Hypatius returned there. When that marzban could not fulfill his promise, because those inside the city would not agree to it, the commander ordered him to be crucified.

The Arabs allied with the Persians came to the Khabur, and Timostratus, the duke of Callinicum, went out against them. (And he routed them.) The Arabs in Roman territory who are called the Banu Tha‘laba also went to Nu‘man's camp and found a caravan traveling up to him. There were also camels carrying provisions up to him. They fell upon them and slaughtered them, and seized the camels. But they did not reach the camp itself, because it had moved into the inner desert. Then, in the month of August, the entire Persian army assembled again, along with the Huns, the Cadiseni, and the Armenians. They came as far as Apadna. Patricius's men heard about this, and he set out to march against them. While the Romans were still on the road and had not yet drawn up for battle, the Persians encountered their advance troops and struck them. When those who had been struck turned back, the rest of the Roman army saw that the advance troops had been defeated, and fear fell upon them. They did not remain to fight. Instead, Patricius was the first to turn back, and the whole army followed him. They crossed the Euphrates River and escaped to the city of Samosata. Nu‘man, the king of the Arabs allied with the Persians, was also wounded in this battle. One of the Roman commanders, whose name was Peter, fled to the fortress of Ashparin. When the Persians surrounded the fortress, its inhabitants became afraid of them and handed him over to them. The Persians took him away in chains and killed the Romans who were with him. But they did no harm to the inhabitants of the fortress.

Kavadh, the king of the Persians, was planning to advance against Areobindus at Edessa. Nu‘man, the king of the Arabs, was also urging him on because of what had happened to his caravan. But one of the troop commanders from Nu‘man's camp, who was a Christian, spoke up and said, “Your Majesty should not trouble yourself to go to war against Edessa, because it has an inviolable promise from Christ, whom they worship, that no enemy will ever gain control of it.” When Nu‘man heard this, he threatened to do worse things in Edessa than had been done in Amida, and he spoke blasphemous words. Christ also displayed a clear sign in him. For at the very time he was blaspheming, the wound he had received in his head became inflamed, and his entire scalp swelled up. He got up and went to his tent. He remained in this agony for two days and died. But not even this sign restrained Kavadh's insolence or turned him from his evil purpose. Instead, he appointed a king in Nu‘man's place and set out to wage war. When he reached Tella, he laid siege to it. The Jews who were there planned to hand the city over to him. They made a hollow in the tower of their synagogue, which had also been entrusted to them to guard. They informed the Persians about it so that they could break through it and enter by it. But this became known to Count Peter, who was being held captive. He persuaded those who were guarding him to bring him near the wall, saying that he had clothing and various kinds of goods stored in the city, and that he wanted to appeal to the people of Tella about these things so that they would give them to him.
