The guards agreed and brought him near. He told the soldiers stationed on the wall to summon Count Leontius, who was guarding the city at that time. They summoned him and the officials. Peter spoke with them in Latin and revealed the Jews’ plot to them. To keep the matter from becoming known to the Persians, he asked them to give him a set of clothes. At first they acted as though they were mocking him. Then they threw him a set of clothes from the wall. For he really did need clothes to wear. Then he came down from the wall. They acted as though they were unaware of the Jews’ plot and did not know where the place was. They went around inspecting the foundations of the entire wall, as though they wanted to see whether it needed repairs. He did this for Peter’s sake, lest the Persians learn that he had disclosed the matter and subject him to further suffering. Finally they came to the place where the Jews were keeping watch, and he found a large excavation dug and prepared for them inside the tower, just as they had been told. When the Romans saw what was there, they attacked them in great fury. They went throughout the city and killed every Jew they found: men, women, old people, and children. They continued doing this for days. Only with difficulty did they stop their slaughter, at Count Leontius’s command and through the persuasion of the blessed Bishop Bar-Hadad. They guarded the city carefully by night and day, while the holy Bar-Hadad went around visiting them, praying over them, and blessing them. He praised their diligence, encouraged them, and sprinkled baptismal water on them and on the city wall. He also carried the Eucharist around with him to give them communion in the mystery at their posts, lest for this reason one of them should leave his watch and come down from the wall. He also went out confidently to the Persian king, spoke with him, and treated him in a friendly way. When Kavadh saw the man’s dignity and also became aware of the Romans’ vigilance, he did not think it advantageous to linger at Tella with the whole army he had with him. For one thing, provisions were unavailable to him in the devastated countryside; for another, he feared that the Roman commanders might gather together and attack him jointly. For these reasons he quickly set out toward Edessa and camped for about twenty days beside the River Jullab, which is called the River of the Medes.

The bold men in his forces went around the countryside, laying it waste. On the sixth day of the month of Elul, the people of Edessa demolished all the monasteries and [?] that were close to the wall. They burned the village of Kfar Selem, which is Negeb. They tore down all the fences of the gardens and orchards around the city and cut down the trees within them. They brought inside the bones of all the martyrs who lay around the city and brought weapons up onto the wall. They fastened haircloth screens above the battlements. On the ninth day of this same month, Kavadh sent word to Areobindus that he should either receive his marzban into the city or come out to meet him on the plain, saying that he wished to establish a treaty of peace with him. But he secretly ordered his army that, if Areobindus allowed them to enter the city, they should turn around and seize its gate and entrance, until he himself came and entered behind them. If Areobindus came outside to meet them, they were to lie in wait for him, seize him alive, and bring him to him. But Areobindus, because he was afraid to allow them to enter the city, went outside to meet them. He did not go far from the city, but only as far as the church of Saint Sergius. Bawi came to him. He was the astabid, which means the Persians’ master of soldiers, and he said to Areobindus, “If you want us to make peace, give us ten thousand pounds of gold, and establish an agreement with us that we will receive the customary gold payment every year.” Areobindus promised to give as much as seven thousand pounds, but they were unwilling to accept it. They continued arguing with him, from morning until the ninth hour. Because he found no opportunity for their treachery, on account of the Romans who were guarding Areobindus, and because they were also afraid to attack Edessa on account of what had happened to Naaman, they left Areobindus in Edessa, and he went to attack Harran. He sent all the Arabs to Sarug. But Rhephius, who was in Harran, secretly went out of the city and fell upon them. He killed sixty of their men and captured the leader of the Huns alive. Because this was a well-known man and highly valued by the Persian king, the king promised the people of Harran that, if they handed him over alive, he would not attack them. They were afraid of war and handed over that Hun. Along with him, they sent fifteen hundred rams and other things as a gift of honor.

The Persian Arabs who had been sent to Sarug went as far as the Euphrates River, devastating the land, taking captives, and plundering everything they found. At this time Patriciolus, one of the Roman commanders, and his son Vitalian had come from the west to go into battle. He was bold and fearless, since he had not yet encountered the things that had happened earlier. When he crossed the river, he encountered one of the Persian commanders and fought him. He destroyed all the Persians who were with that commander. He set out toward Edessa, but heard from fugitives that Kavadh had surrounded the city. He turned back, crossed the river, and at Samosata [?]. On the seventeenth day of this month, a Wednesday, we saw Christ’s words and his promises to Abgar being fulfilled in deed. For Kavadh gathered his entire army, set out from the Euphrates River, and came and encamped against Edessa. His camp extended from the martyrs’ shrine of Saint Cosmas and Saint Damian, with his troops occupying all the gardens, the church of Saint Sergius, and the village of Bekin, as far as Beth Maudana. Its breadth extended as far as Shahrta of Tsarin. This whole countless army surrounded Edessa during the day, besides the guards he had stationed in the mountains and on the heights. The entire plain was full of them. All the city’s gates were open, yet the Persians could not enter it because of Christ’s blessing. Instead, fear fell upon them, and they remained in their positions, although no one was fighting them, from morning until about the ninth hour. Then a few men went out of the city and fought them. They killed many Persians, while only one of their own men fell. The women were carrying water and bringing it outside the wall for those who were fighting to drink. Young boys were throwing stones with slings. A few men who came out of the city therefore drove them away and forced them back from the wall. For they were not far from it, but only about a bowshot away. They went and camped beside the village of Qubbe.

Later in the day, Areobindus again went outside the great gate. Standing opposite the Persian army, he sent this message to Kavadh: “Now you have learned by experience that the city is neither yours nor Anastasius’s. Rather, it is the city of Christ, who blessed it and stood against your armies to prevent them from gaining control of it.” Kavadh sent him this reply: “Give me hostages to guarantee that you will not pursue me when I depart, and send me those men whom you captured yesterday, and the gold you promised, and I will withdraw from the city.” Areobindus handed over to him Count Basil and the men who had been captured from his army, who numbered fourteen men. He also made an agreement with him to give him two thousand pounds of gold within twelve days. Kavadh departed and went to camp at Dahbana. But he did not wait for the appointed deadline. Instead, on the following day he sent one of his men, named Hormizd, and instructed him to bring back three hundred pounds of gold. Areobindus gathered the leading men of the city around him to consider how that gold could be collected. When they saw that Hormizd had come so soon, they drew strength from their trust in Christ, took courage, and said to Areobindus, “We will not send gold to a liar. For just as he has gone back on his word and has not waited until the day you appointed for him, so he will go back on it and act deceitfully when he has received the gold. We believe that if he fights against us again, he will be put to shame, because Christ stands in defense of his city.” Then Areobindus too took courage and sent this message to Kavadh: “Now we know that you are not a king, for no king gives his word and then goes back on it deceitfully. If he does act deceitfully, he is not a king. Now that you have shown yourself deceitful, send Count Basil back to me, and do whatever is in your power to do.”

Then Kavadh became enraged. He equipped the elephants he had with him for battle, set out with his entire army, and came again to fight against Edessa, on the twenty-fourth day of the month of September, a Wednesday. He surrounded the city on all sides, more closely than before, while all its gates stood open. Areobindus had ordered the Romans not to fight against him, so that no deceit should be apparent on his own part. But a few villagers who were in the city went out against him with slings. They struck down many of the armored men with him, while not a single one of their own fell. His legions were making bold attempts to enter the city, but whenever they approached its gates, like a towering wave at the sand, they subsided, hesitated, and turned back. Because of the speed at which their horses galloped, the slingers mingled among them. Although the Persians were shooting arrows, the Huns were brandishing clubs, and the Arabs were leveling spears against them, they could not wound a single one of them. Rather, they were like those Philistines who came up against Samson: although they were very numerous and armed, they could not kill him. But he, though unarmed, killed a thousand of them with a donkey’s jawbone. Likewise, the Persians, Huns, and Arabs, though they and their horses were falling under the stones thrown by the slingers, could not kill even one of them. When they saw that they could neither enter the city nor harm the unarmed men mingling among them, they set fire to the church of Saint Sergius and the church of the Confessors, and to all the monasteries that remained, and to the southern church, for the city’s inhabitants had spared this one.

When Areobindus, the commander, saw the villagers’ zeal, and that they had not [?], and the help that had accompanied them, he gathered all the villagers who were in Edessa into the church in the afternoon and gave them gifts amounting to three hundred dinars. Kavad departed from Edessa and went and camped beside the Euphrates River. From there he sent messengers to the emperor to inform him of his coming. The Arabs who were with him crossed the river westward and plundered, devastated, took captives, and burned everything they found. A small force of Persian cavalry went to Batnae. Because its wall had been breached, the inhabitants could not resist them. Instead, they received them without a battle and surrendered the city to them.

The year eight hundred and fifteen. When the Roman emperor learned what had happened, he sent Celer, his master of offices, with a large army. When Kavad heard this, he made his marches along the Euphrates River, intending to go and settle in his own territory, which is called Beth Aramaye. As he approached Callinicum, he sent a marzban there to fight against them. Duke Timostratus went out against him and destroyed his entire force, and captured him alive. When Kavad reached the city, he drew up his entire army against it, threatening to destroy it and subject all its inhabitants to the sword and captivity unless they handed the man over to him. The duke was afraid of the size of the Persian army and handed him over.

When Celer, the master of offices, reached Mabbog on the Euphrates River and saw that Kavad had withdrawn before him, and that winter had now arrived, so that he could not pursue him, he summoned the Roman commanders and dismissed them because they had not obeyed one another. He assigned them cities in which to spend the winter until the time for battle came.

On the twenty-fifth of December, an order came from the emperor that the tax should be remitted throughout Mesopotamia. When the Persians who were in Amida saw that the Roman army had moved far away from them, they opened the gates of the city of Amida. They went out and came in wherever they wished. They sold merchants copper, lead, iron, [?] utensils, and everything that could be found in the city. They also established [?] there. When Patricius heard this, he departed from Melitene, where he was spending the winter, and came and encamped outside Amida. He killed all the merchants he found bringing grain and oil there, as well as those buying goods from there. He also found the Persians whom Kavad had sent to bring weapons, grain, and livestock there, and destroyed them. He took everything they had with them. When Kavad learned of this, he sent a marzban against him to take revenge on him. When they drew near one another to fight, the Romans, afraid because of their earlier defeat, advised Patricius to flee. He followed this advice. In their haste, not knowing where they were going, they came upon a river called Callat. Because it was winter and the river was in full flood, they could not cross it. Every one of them who hurried to cross the river drowned along with his horse. When Patricius saw this, he encouraged the Romans, saying: “Roman soldiers, let us not disgrace our ancestry and our military service by fleeing from our enemies. Instead, let us turn against them; perhaps we can withstand their strength. But if they overpower us, it is better to die by the sword with a good reputation for bravery than to perish like cowards, drowned in the water.” Then the Romans accepted his advice because of the predicament the river presented. They turned against the Persians in fury and put them to the sword. They captured their commanders alive. Afterward they turned back and advanced against Amida. Patricius sent for craftsmen from other cities and gathered them to himself, along with many villagers. He ordered them to dig into the ground and make a tunnel beneath the wall so that it would give way and fall.

In the month of Adar, while the rest of the Romans were assembling to go down with the magister, a certain sign was given to them by God to encourage them and make them confident of victory. We learned about it in writing from the members of the church of Zeugma. So that you do not think I am saying anything on my own authority, or that I have been persuaded to endorse a false report, I set down the very words of the letter that reached us. They are as follows:

“Hear, then, of a marvel and a glorious joy unlike anything that has happened before. For this belongs to us, to you, and to all the Romans. It is an astonishing event, one that the minds of mortal people find difficult to believe. But we have seen it with our own eyes, held it, and read it aloud with our own lips. You ought to believe it without any hesitation. On the nineteenth of Adar, a Friday, which is the day our Savior was killed, a goose laid an egg in Agar, a village in the district of Zeugma. On it are beautiful, legible Greek letters. They are of the same substance as the egg itself and stand out both to sight and to touch, like the letters that monks inscribe on loaves of blessed bread. Even blind people can feel their shapes. They are as follows: a cross is marked on the side of the egg. Starting from it, the inscription runs around the egg until it reaches the cross again. It reads, ‘The Romans.’ Another cross is also marked, and from it, until the inscription comes back to it, is written, ‘Are victorious.’ The crosses are marked one above the other, and the words are written one above the other. No Christian or Jew who sees this marvel can keep his mouth from offering praise. We do not dare to imitate the letters that God’s right hand wrote within the womb, for they are exceedingly beautiful. So assure everyone who hears of it without any doubt.” These are the words of the letter from the people of Zeugma. The people in whose village the egg had been laid gave it to Areobindus.

The Romans assembled a large army and went down and encamped near the city of Rhesaina. About ten thousand men were also sent by Kavadh to march against Patricius. They came and camped at Nisibis to rest there. They sent their livestock to graze on Mount Singara. When the master of the soldiers heard this, he sent Timostratus, the duke of Callinicum, with six thousand cavalry. They went, and he fell upon those who were tending the horses and slaughtered them. He took away horses, sheep, and a great deal of plunder from there. He returned to the Roman army at Reshaina. Then they all set out together and went and encamped by the city of Amida, alongside Patricius.

In the month of May, Calliopius of Aleppo became prefect. He came and stayed at Edessa and gave wheat to the Edessenes so that they could make hardtack at their own expense. During this time they baked eight hundred and fifty thousand modii of wheat. Apion went to Alexandria to have hardtack made there too and to send bread.

Meanwhile, as Patricius advanced through the tunnel he had dug beneath the wall of Amida, he supported it with timbers and set them on fire. The outer face of the wall gave way and fell, but the inner face remained standing. He decided to dig through that same tunnel and enter the city. When he broke through the tunnel and the Romans began to climb up, a woman from Amida saw them. In her joy she suddenly cried out, “Look, the Romans are entering the city!” The Persians heard her and rushed at the first man who came up and stabbed him. After him came up a Goth named Ald, who had been appointed tribune at Harran. He stabbed three of those Persians. No other Roman came up after him, because the Persians had become aware of them. When Ald saw that no one was coming up, he became afraid and turned back. He decided to take down with him the body of the Roman who had fallen, so that the Persians would not mock it. As he dragged the body and descended into the mouth of the tunnel, the Persians struck him too and wounded him. They diverted water there from the large spring nearby, and four of the armored Romans who were preparing to climb up drowned there. The rest fled and escaped from there. The Persians gathered stones from inside the city and blocked the tunnel. They piled a great deal of earth over it and carefully guarded the whole area around it, in case a passage should be broken through somewhere else. They dug trenches on the inside, all the way around the wall, and filled them with water, so that if the Romans made another tunnel, the water would flow into it and it would be discovered. When Patricius learned this from a deserter who came down to him, he gave up tunneling.

One day, while the whole Roman army was encamped and at rest, an occasion for battle arose in this way. A boy was tending camels and donkeys. As one donkey grazed, it wandered off and came close to the wall. The boy was afraid to go in and fetch it. When one of the Persians saw it, he came down from the wall on a rope. He wanted to cut it up and take it up so that they could have it for food. For there was no meat at all inside the city. But one of the Roman soldiers, who was a Galilean by birth, drew his sword, took his shield in his left hand, and ran at the Persian to kill him. And because he was approaching the wall, Those standing on top of the wall threw down a large stone and crushed that Galilean. The Persian began climbing back up to his position by a rope. When he reached halfway up the wall, one of the Roman commanders approached, with two shield-bearers walking ahead of him, and shot an arrow from between them. He struck that Persian and knocked him down beside the Galilean. A shout went up from both sides. This stirred them up, and they rose to fight. All the Roman forces were gathered closely together around the city. Forty of their men fell, and a hundred and fifty were wounded. Of the Persians on the wall, only nine were seen to have died, and few were wounded. For it was difficult to fight them while they were high up on the wall, because they had also built small shelters for themselves along the whole wall. They stood inside these and fought, without being visible to those outside.

But the master of the soldiers and the military commanders decided that they should not fight them, because killing them would not bring victory to the Romans, since they still faced a war against all the Persians. If Kavadh were defeated, these men would surrender or perish in their confinement. For this reason he ordered that no one should fight them, lest the main body of the army become disheartened because of the Romans who were killed or wounded.

In the month of June, Constantine, who had gone over to the Persians, saw that their cause was not succeeding and fled from them, together with two prominent women from Amida who had been given to him by the Persian king. For fourteen days he traveled night and day through an uninhabited desert with the few people accompanying him. When he reached safety, he made himself known to the Arabs allied with the Romans. They took him and brought him to the fortress called Sura, and from there they sent him to Edessa. When the emperor heard of his arrival, he sent for him. When he arrived to appear before him, the emperor ordered one of the bishops to lay hands on him and ordain him a priest. He was to go and live in the city of Nicaea, never appear before the emperor, and take no part in public affairs.

Now Kavadh, because after capturing Amida he had also entered its public baths and experienced the benefit of bathing, had ordered, as soon as he returned to his own country, that bathhouses should be built in all the towns of Persia. Adid, an Arab under Persian authority, surrendered with his entire force and submitted to the Romans. Again, in the month of July, the Romans fought the Persians in Amida. Gainas, the duke of Arabia, struck many of them with arrows. When the day grew hot, his armor became burning hot on him, and he loosened the fastening of his breastplate a little. They shot bolts from ballistas in Amida and struck him, and he died. When the master of the soldiers saw that his siege of Amida was causing him losses, he took his army and went down into Persian territory. He left Patricius near Amida. Areobindus also took his army and entered Persian Armenia. He killed ten thousand Armenian and Persian men, and they took thirty thousand women and children captive. They plundered and burned many villages. When they turned back toward Amida, they drove away 120,000 sheep, cattle, and other livestock. As they were passing beside the city of Nisibis, the Romans lay in ambush. They sent the captives past with only a few men accompanying them. When a marzban who was there saw that they were few, he armed his troops and went out to take the captives away from them. They pretended to flee, and the Persians took courage and pursued them. When he had gone some distance from them, the Romans rose from their ambush and slaughtered them. Not one of them escaped. There were about seven thousand men. Mushegh the Armenian, who was under Persian authority, also surrendered with his entire army and submitted to the Romans.

The year eight hundred and sixteen. The survivors among the inhabitants of Amida who had escaped the sword and remained there were suffering great distress and torment from hunger. For the Persians feared that they might hand the city over to the Romans. They bound all the men who were there and threw them into the arena. Thus they perished from hunger and also in their bonds [?]. They gave the women some of their food because they were having sexual relations with them, and also because they needed them to grind grain and bake for them. When their provisions ran short, they despised the women and left them without food. For during that year each of them received only a handful of barley a day. They had absolutely no meat, wine, or any other food. Because they were very afraid of the Romans, they never left their guard posts at all. Instead, he made small ovens for them on the wall and brought hand mills up for them. At their posts they ground that handful of barley, baked it, and ate it. He also brought up large kneading troughs and placed them [?], and they filled them with earth. They sowed vegetables in them and ate whatever grew in them.

An account of what the women there were doing may perhaps be believed by those who come after us. Today there is no one eager to learn about events who has not heard everything that happened, even if he lives very far away from us. Many women therefore gathered together and made secret agreements among themselves. They would go out secretly into the city streets, in the evening or the morning. Whoever they found—whether a woman, a child, [or an old man]—whom they could overpower, they would drag into a house, kill, and eat, either boiled or roasted. When this was exposed by the smell of roasting meat and the matter became known to the marzban who was there, he tortured many of them and killed them. He threatened those who remained, telling them not to do this again or kill anyone. But he permitted them to eat those who died, and they did this openly. They ate the flesh of dead people. The rest of the women gathered shoes from their feet, worn-out leather, and disgusting things from the streets and courtyards, and ate them. The Roman armies, however, lacked nothing. [?] Everything was supplied to them at the proper time, coming down by the king’s command with great care. Goods for sale were more plentiful in their camps than in the cities [?]: food, drink, footwear, and clothing. All the cities had hard bread baked by bakers and sent it to them. Especially the people of Edessa. For this year too, the townspeople baked in their courtyards at the command of Calliopius the governor: Six hundred and thirty thousand measures, apart from what was baked by the villages throughout the district and by foreign and local bakers.

This year Lord Peter, the bishop, again went up to the king to persuade him to remit the tax. The king answered him harshly and reproached him for abandoning the care of the poor at such a time and coming up to him. For he said that God himself had put it into his heart, if it was right, to do good to the blessed city without anyone’s appeal. While the bishop was still there, the king sent a remission to all Mesopotamia through someone else, without the bishop’s knowledge. For the district of Mabbug too, he remitted one third of the tax.

The Roman commanders who were besieging Amida used to make raids into Persian territory, plundering, taking captives, and laying waste. The Persians fled before them and crossed the River Tigris. There they found Persian cavalry assembling to attack the Romans. They took courage because of them and remained on the far side of the Tigris. The Romans crossed after them and slaughtered all the Persian cavalry, who numbered about ten thousand men. They plundered all the property of those who had fled, burned many villages, and killed every male in them from twelve years old and upward. They took the women and children captive. For the master of soldiers had given all the commanders this order: If any Roman was found sparing a male twelve years old or older, he himself was to be killed in his place. And in every village they entered, they were not to leave even a single house standing. For this purpose he selected strong men from among the Romans and many villagers, who accompanied them when they went down. After the roofs had burned and the fire had gone out, they pulled down even the walls. They also cut down and destroyed the vineyards, olive trees, and all the other trees. The Arabs on the Roman side also crossed the Tigris ahead of them, plundering, taking captives, and destroying everything they found in Persian territory. Since I know that you examine everything thoughtfully, let Your Holiness consider this too: This war was a source of great profit for the Arabs on both sides, and it fulfilled their desires in both kingdoms.

When Kavadh saw that the Romans were devastating his country and that no one was standing against them, he wanted to come out to confront them. For this reason he sent Astabid to the master of soldiers to discuss peace. He had with him a force of about twenty thousand. He also sent all the prominent men whom he had taken captive from Amida, and Peter, whom he had carried off from Ashparin, and Basil, whom he had taken from Edessa as a hostage. He had also sent back the body of Duke Olympius, who had gone down to him as an envoy and died there, in a sealed coffin. This was to show that he had died a natural death and nothing else. His servants and those who had gone down with him testified to this. The magister took them and sent them to Edessa, except for the governor of Amida and Count Peter. For he was angry and furious, and wanted to punish them. For he believed that the positions they had been guarding had been surrendered through their negligence. The Persians themselves testified in support of this that the wall of Amida was impregnable. Astabid, however, asked him and pleaded with him to give him the Persians imprisoned in Amida in exchange for these men whom he had brought. For although they were holding out because of their fear of them, they were suffering severely from hunger. But the magister said, “Let the business of these men be my concern, because they are confined in our city and are our slaves.” Astabid said to him, “Then let me send them provisions. For it is not fitting for your slaves to perish from hunger. Whenever you wish, it is easy for you to kill them.” He said to him, “Send them.” Astabid said, “Swear to me, you and all the commanders and officers with you, that no one will kill the men I send.” They all swore to him, except Duke Nonnus, who was not with them in person. For the magister had left him behind for this very reason, so that if there were any oath, he would not be bound by it. Astabid therefore sent three hundred camels carrying sacks of bread. Arrows had been placed inside them. Nonnus attacked them and took these things from them, and killed the men who were with them. When Astabid complained about this and questioned the magister, [?] “I cannot find out who did this, because of the great number of troops with me. But if you know who it was and have the strength to take revenge on him, I will not stop you.” Astabid was frightened by this and pleaded for peace.

After many days had passed while he was pleading, there was severe cold, with much snow and ice. The Romans left their camps one by one. Each man took whatever share of the plunder had fallen to him and went to carry it home. Those who remained and did not go home entered Tella, Reshaina, and Edessa to shelter from the cold. When Astabid saw that the Romans had grown weak and could not endure exposure to the weather, he sent word to the magister, “Either make peace and let the Persians leave Amida, or accept battle.” The magister ordered Count Justin to assemble the army, but he could not. When he saw that most of the Romans had dispersed from his command, he made peace and allowed the Persians to leave Amida, on the condition that both kings should approve and ratify what he had done; otherwise, war would continue between them. When the Roman emperor learned what had happened, he ordered that [?] be established in all the cities, and especially in Amida. And in order to end the hostility and urge him toward peace, he sent honors and gifts to Kavadh through a man named Leo, along with a complete set of gold vessels for serving his table.

No one knows how much the people of Edessa who transported grain to Amida suffered, except those who were themselves involved in the undertaking. For many of them died on the road, both the men and their pack animals.

The virtuous John, bishop of Amida, had passed away before the Persians laid siege to it. His clergy went up to the holy, God-loving, devoted, and illustrious Mar Flavian, patriarch of Antioch, who was adorned with every divine virtue, so that he might appoint a bishop for them. He treated them with honor throughout their stay there. Afterward, the excellent Nonnus, a priest and steward of his church in Amid, escaped from captivity. The clergy petitioned the patriarch, and he made him their bishop. When this excellent Nonnus had assumed the office of bishop, he sent Thomas, his rural bishop, to Constantinople to take charge of the people of Amid [?] who were there and to request a grant from the emperor. Those who were there reached an agreement with him and petitioned the emperor that this Thomas should become their bishop. The emperor accepted their petition and wrote to the patriarch not to oppose them. The emperor also gave them the judge he requested. The emperor and the patriarch gave gifts to the church of Amid, as well as a large amount of gold for him to distribute to the poor. Because of this, all those who had been wandering in other regions gathered there. Every day they carried the bodies of the dead out of Amid, and then received what had been allotted to them.

Urbicius, the emperor’s eunuch, who had performed great acts of charity in the region of Jerusalem and elsewhere, also went down there and gave out a dinar to each person. From there he came to Edessa and gave a tremissis to every woman who wished to receive one, and one silver coin to every child. Almost all the women received it, both those who were in need and those who were not.

In this same year, after the war had ended, wild beasts attacked us. Because of the many corpses that had fallen in those battles [?], they had become accustomed to eating human bodies. When the bodies of the slain had decayed and disappeared, the beasts began entering the villages, snatching children and eating them. They also attacked men traveling alone on the roads and tore them apart. People were so afraid that at threshing time no one in the entire district would spend the night at his threshing floor without a raised shelter, for fear of the ferocious beasts. But with the help of our Lord, who always cares for us and in his mercy rescues us from all our trials, some of them fell into the hands of the villagers, who stabbed them. They sent their dead bodies to Edessa. Hunters also caught some of them, bound them, and brought them in alive. Everyone saw them and praised God, who said, “I will put the fear and dread of you upon every beast of the earth.” For although, because of our sins, the sword, famine, pestilence, captivity, wild beasts, and other punishments, both recorded and unrecorded, were sent upon us, in his grace he delivered us from them all.

Through your prayers, his mercy also gave strength to me, insignificant as I am, to write, as far as I could, about some of the things that happened, in remembrance of those who endured them and for the instruction of those who come after us. If they wish, they can gain wisdom from these few things I have written. For the things I have left out are more numerous than those I have written down. Indeed, I said at the beginning that I was not capable of recording them all. For if the sufferings endured by each individual person were written down, they would make lengthy histories. Even a large book would not be enough to contain them. You can learn about these things from what others are recording. Even those who came to help us under the name of saviors plundered us almost like enemies, both as they came down and as they went back up. For they drove many poor people out of their beds and slept in them themselves, while their owners lay stretched out on the ground in the cold weather. They drove others out of their houses, entered them, and lodged there. They forcibly led away some people's livestock as though it were booty. They stripped the clothing of [?] from their bodies and took it away. They treated others with harsh blows over any matter whatsoever. They brought accusations against others in the marketplaces and caused them losses over some trifling matter. They openly plundered everyone's scant food and whatever supplies individuals had in the villages and towns. They also attacked many people along the roads. Since the courtyards and inns of the city were not sufficient for them, they lodged with craftsmen in their shops. In full view of everyone, they abused women in the streets and houses. They took oil, firewood, salt, and other things for their own use from elderly women, widows, and poor women. By making these women serve them, they kept them from their work. In short, they oppressed everyone, great and small. No one was left untouched by their wickedness. Even the local officials appointed to organize and quarter them had their hands stretched out for bribes, and although from everyone they took payments, they spared no one. Instead, after a few days they sent others to those from whose houses they had previously removed men. They even lodged with priests and deacons, although these had an imperial document forbidding anyone to quarter troops with them. Why should I weary myself by listing so many things? Perhaps even those greater than I could not manage it.

After crossing the River Euphrates westward, the master of soldiers went to the emperor, Areobindus to Antioch, Patricius to Melitene, Pharzman to Apamea, Theodore to Damascus, and Calliopius to Mabbug. There was a little relief in Edessa, and the small number of men remaining in it brought it some comfort. Eulogius the governor took care to rebuild it [?] The emperor [?] two hundred pounds for the building expenses. He built and restored [?] the outer wall that surrounded the city. He also restored and repaired the two aqueducts that came in from the village of Tell-Zema and from Maudad. He also rebuilt and completed the public bath that had collapsed. He also restored his own praetorium and did much building throughout the city. The emperor also gave the bishop twenty pounds for the expenses of restoring the wall. And Urbicius the eunuch gave ten pounds to build a martyrs' shrine for the blessed Mary. The oil available amounted to six thousand eight hundred sextarii. The governor took it from them and ordered it to be used to light the city's colonnades. The shrine custodians pleaded with him earnestly about it, but he would not be persuaded. So that he would not be thought to despise the sanctuaries built for God, he gave two hundred sextarii from his own resources to each martyrs' shrine. At this time of the year, four modii of wheat were being sold for a dinar, and six of barley. Wine sold at two measures for a dinar. After the new harvest, six modii of wheat were sold for a dinar, and ten of barley.

The Arabs allied with the Persians, however, did not stop or remain quiet. Instead, they crossed into Roman territory without the Persians' permission. They took the inhabitants of two villages captive. When the Persian marzban stationed at Nisibis learned of this, he seized their leaders and killed them. The Arabs in Roman territory also crossed into Persian territory without orders and took the people of an estate captive. When news of this affair reached the master of soldiers—for he had gone down to Apamea at the end of this year— he sent word to Timostratus, the duke of Callinicum. He seized five of their leaders, killed two of them with the sword, and crucified three on wooden crosses. Pharasmanes left Apamea after the master of the army had gone down there, and came to stay in Edessa. He received authority from the emperor to be commander of the army in place of Hypatius.

The wall of Batnae, the fortress in Sarug, which had fallen and was breached throughout, was rebuilt and restored through the efforts of Eulogius, governor of Edessa. The excellent priest Hadas covered the doors of the men's section of the church of Edessa with bronze.

The year eight hundred and seventeen. The commanders of the Roman army informed the emperor that the troops were suffering great harm because they had no city situated on the frontier. For whenever the Romans went out from Tella or Amida to patrol the region of Arab because of raiding bands, they were in danger wherever they camped because of the enemy's schemes. And if they happened to encounter forces more numerous than their own and considered turning back, they endured great hardship because there was no city nearby in which they could take shelter. For this reason the emperor ordered a wall to be built around the village of Dara, which stands on the frontier. Stonecutters were selected from throughout Syria and went down there to build it. But the Persians used to come out from Nisibis and hinder them. For this reason Pharasmanes left Edessa and went down to stay in Amida. He would go out to the builders and help them. He also conducted great hunts of wild animals, especially wild boars, which had multiplied there since the region had been devastated. He would hunt more than forty of them in a single day. As a demonstration of his skill in hunting, he even sent some of them to Edessa, both living and dead.

The excellent Sergius, bishop of Birtha, the fortress near us on the Euphrates River, also began building a wall around his city. The emperor gave him a considerable amount of gold for its expenses. The master of the army also ordered a wall to be built around Europus, which stands west of the river in the province of Hierapolis. The local inhabitants worked on it as their strength allowed.

After Pharasmanes went down to Amida, Duke Romanus came in his place and stayed in Edessa with his army. He gave abundant alms to the poor. In addition to all his other good deeds, the emperor also sent a remission of the land tax to all Mesopotamia in this year. All the estate owners rejoiced and praised the emperor.

But the common people grumbled and cried out, saying, "The Goths should not be quartered on us, but on the estate owners, since they are the ones who have benefited from this remission." The governor ordered that their request be granted. When this began to be carried out, all the leading men of the city gathered before Duke Romanus and appealed to him, saying, "Let Your Excellency prescribe what each of the Goths should receive each month, lest, when they enter the houses of respectable [?] people, they plunder them as they have been plundering the common people." He accepted their appeal and ordered that they should receive a measure [?] of oil each month, two hundred pounds of firewood, and a bed and bedding for every two of them.

When the Goths heard this order, they rushed at Duke Romanus in the courtyard of the house of Barsa to kill him. As they were coming up the stairs of his lodging, he heard the noise of their uproar and commotion and realized what they intended to do. He quickly put on his armor, took up his weapons, drew his sword, and stood at the upper doorway of the place where they were staying. He did not kill a single Goth, but brandished his sword and prevented those at the front of the ascending crowd from entering and attacking him. Those below, in their fury, were forcing those above them to go up and enter to attack them. Now the stairways of that courtyard held a great many people, as Your Holiness knows. So when those who had gone up first could not enter because they feared the sword, and those behind were pressing against them, many men crowded onto the stairs. Under their weight, the stairway broke and fell on them. A few of them died, and many suffered injuries to their limbs and were left disabled. They never recovered. When this collapse gave Romanus an opportunity, he escaped over the roof from one courtyard to another and got away. He said nothing more to them. For this reason they remained where they were quartered, behaving as they pleased. There was no one to discipline them, restrain them, or admonish them.

Our bishop, Mar Peter, suffered from a severe and distressing illness throughout this year. In the month of Nisan, the distress of our city grew still worse. Celer [?], the master of soldiers, assembled the entire army. He set out to go down to Persian territory to establish and renew a peace treaty with them. When he entered Edessa, Persian envoys came to him and informed him that the Astabid who was coming to meet him to establish a treaty with him had died. They appealed to him, saying that if he had come down to make peace, he ought not to go beyond Edessa until another Astabid had been sent by the Persian king. He accepted their request and stayed in Edessa for five months. Since the city could not accommodate the Goths who were with him, they were also quartered in the villages. The same was true of all the large monasteries around the city. Not even those who lived in solitude were allowed to remain in the quiet they loved, for the soldiers were also quartered upon them in their monasteries.

Because they were not eating at their own expense, they indulged so excessively in food and drink on the first day they arrived that some of them, after feasting in upper rooms, went out at night, confused by the great quantity of wine. They stepped into empty space and plunged down. Thus they departed this life with a miserable end. Others, while sitting and drinking, sank into sleep, fell from the upper rooms, and died on the spot. Others burned up in their beds from excessive eating. Others poured boiling [?] into the ears of those who served them for minor faults. Others entered a garden to take vegetables. When the gardener stood up to prevent them from taking them, one of them dealt him death with an arrow. His blood was not avenged. Others, as their wickedness increased and there was no one to discipline them, although the people with whom they were quartered behaved very considerately toward them and did everything as they wished, giving them no grounds for harming them, were overcome by their own fury and killed one another. You are aware, however, that there were also others among them who lived in an orderly manner. For it is impossible that an army as large as that should not contain such men as well. The wickedness of the bad men became so violent in its wrongdoing that even those among the Edessenes who were bold dared to do something improper. They wrote accusations against the master of soldiers on sheets of paper and secretly posted them in prominent places in the city. When he heard about this, however, he did not become angry, as he might have done. He did not investigate who had done it, nor, because of his kindness, did he consider doing any harm to the city. Instead, he took great pains to leave Edessa quickly and without delay.

The year eight hundred and eighteen. The master of soldiers then took his entire army and went down to the frontier. A Persian envoy came to him at the city of Dara, bringing with him hostages who had been sent by the Astabid. Once again they appealed to him. If he wished to make peace, he too ought to send hostages in exchange for those he had received. Afterward, the two sides would approach one another in friendship. They would meet one another with five hundred horsemen on each side, unarmed. Then they would sit in conference and do what was necessary. He accepted their proposal and sent hostages. On the day appointed for him, he went unarmed to meet Astabid. But because he feared that the Persians might attempt some treachery against him, he stationed the entire Roman army opposite them, fully armed. He gave them a signal and ordered them to come to him quickly if they saw that signal. When Astabid also came to meet him and sat in conference, those Romans and all the commanders with them [?]. One of the Roman soldiers noticed and saw that everyone who had come with Astabid was wearing armor underneath. He reported this to Pharzman, the army commander, and to Timostratus, the duke. They showed the signal to the troops, who immediately raised a battle cry and came up to them. They surrounded Astabid and those with him. When the troops in the Persian camp learned that Astabid and his companions had been surrounded, they fled in fear. They entered Nisibis. The Romans wanted to seize Astabid and kill those with him. The master of the soldiers urged them not to become a cause of war and obstruct peace. Only with difficulty did they agree. They listened to him and allowed Astabid and his companions to leave their midst without harming them in any way. For the Roman commanders are peacemakers even in victory. When Astabid returned to his camp and saw that the Persians had gone into Nisibis, they were afraid to leave the city with him. Because of their fear of the Romans, Astabid sent for his daughter and brought her to Nisibis. In accordance with Persian custom, he took her as his wife. When the master of the soldiers sent him sworn assurances, saying, “No one will harm you, even if you come out alone,” he replied, “It is not out of fear that I am not coming out, but so that the days of the wedding feast may be completed.” Although the master of the soldiers was fully aware of the whole affair, he let it pass as though he did not know.

After [?] days, when Astabid came out to him, he set aside, out of his love of peace, all the grievances for which he had grounds to demand satisfaction from the Persians. He established an agreement with them and made peace, and they drew up a written document between them. In it they fixed a definite period during which they would not wage war against one another. All the troops were glad and rejoiced at the peace that had been made.

While they were still there on the frontier, Celer, the master of the soldiers, and Calliopius received letters from Emperor Anastasius. These were full of concern and compassion for the whole region of Mesopotamia. He wrote to them as follows: if they judged that the tax ought to be remitted, they were to have authority to remit it without delay. They decided that the entire tax should be remitted for the people of Amida, and half of it for the people of Edessa. They sent word of this to Edessa. A little later they also sent other letters [?] announcing the peace that had been made.

On the twenty-eighth day of November, he took the entire army and withdrew from the frontier. When he reached Edessa, the master of the soldiers intended not to enter it because of their complaints against him. But the blessed Bar-Hadad, bishop of Tella, bishop of Tella, persuaded him not to allow anger to gain control over him. And he should not leave distress or anxiety behind him for anyone. He readily accepted his appeal. All the people of Edessa also went out to meet him with great cheerfulness, carrying candles [?], and the people went out with them. He entered the city with joy [?]. He sent the entire army on its way that same day, but he himself stayed for three days and gave the governor two hundred dinars to distribute as gifts. The inhabitants of the city, rejoicing in the peace that had come, delighted at the relief they would now have from the distress they were enduring, and exulting in the hope of the good things they expected to come, gave thanks to God, who in his grace and mercy had bestowed his peace upon both kingdoms, with praises worthy of him. And they escorted the man he had sent as he set out.

If this king should prove to be different at the end of his life, let no one take offense at the praises given to him. Instead, let him remember what Solomon did toward the end of his life. These few things out of many I have written for your beloved self as well as I could, both unwillingly and willingly: unwillingly, so that I would not weary a wise and knowledgeable man who is better informed about these very matters than I am; but willingly, out of obedience to your command. And now I ask that you too fulfill the promise in your letter, that you will continually offer prayer to God for my sinfulness. For now that I have learned your wish, I will take care to record whatever happens in the time to come that is worthy of remembrance, and send it to your fatherhood, if I remain alive. Let us pray from here, and your fatherhood from there, and all people everywhere, that the subject of the history may be the great change that has taken place in the world, and that, just as we have been unable to recount the events of the evil time as they really were because of their many troubles, we may likewise be unable to recount the things to come because of their many blessings. We may likewise be unable to recount the things to come because of their many blessings. Instead, may our account fall short of describing the good conduct of the inhabitants of our city and the peace and harmony that reign in the world, and the great plenty that has come, and the prosperity. [?] May the former troubles also be held in contempt in my eyes. To him be glory forever and ever. Amen.
The end.
